rationale: 'Understand information and ideas presented through spoken words and sentences' is language understanding, which 'pattern-matching ... classification ... retrieval' describes only loosely, and no facet definition names comprehension.

'Read and understand information and ideas presented in writing' is language understanding, which 'pattern-matching ... classification ... retrieval' describes only loosely, and no facet definition names comprehension.
'Communicate information and ideas in speaking' is a kind of 'generation', but the aim 'so others will understand' is not covered by 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Communicate information and ideas in writing' is a kind of 'generation', but the aim 'so others will understand' is not covered by 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Come up with a number of ideas' where 'the number of ideas is important, not their quality' is plainly 'generation' 'at scale'.
'Come up with ... ideas' matches 'generation', but the defining 'unusual or clever ideas' and 'creative ways to solve a problem' are not described by 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Tell when something is wrong' and 'only recognizing that there is a problem' are 'plausibility auditing', and 'likely to go wrong' also touches 'prediction'.

'Apply general rules to specific problems to produce answers that make sense' is rule-based inference, which no definition describes: it is not 'statistical pattern-matching' and not 'causal structure' or 'counterfactual reasoning'.

'Combine pieces of information to form general rules or conclusions' and 'finding a relationship among seemingly unrelated events' are partly 'pattern-matching', and a relationship among events touches 'causal structure'.
'Arrange things or actions in a certain order or pattern according to a specific rule' shares the idea of pattern with 'pattern-matching' but is rule-following, so the match is poor.
'Combining or grouping things' is 'classification', but 'generate or use different sets of rules' for grouping in different ways goes beyond 'statistical pattern-matching'.

'Choose the right mathematical methods or formulas to solve a problem' is method selection for solving, which no definition describes; it is neither 'problem formulation' nor 'variable selection' nor 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Add, subtract, multiply, or divide quickly and correctly' is exact arithmetic, which no definition describes, including 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Remember information such as words, numbers, pictures, and procedures' matches 'retrieval', but holding information in memory is not otherwise 'statistical pattern-matching'.
'Make sense of, combine, and organize information into meaningful patterns' is plainly 'pattern-matching'.
'Identify or detect a known pattern ... hidden in other distracting material' is plainly 'pattern-matching' and 'classification'.

'Compare similarities and differences among sets of letters, numbers, objects, pictures, or patterns' and 'comparing a presented object with a remembered object' are plainly 'pattern-matching' and 'retrieval'.
'Know your location in relation to the environment' and where objects are 'in relation to you' is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.

'Imagine how something will look after it is moved around' concerns physical objects, covered in part by 'sensorimotor intelligence', and imagining the result of parts being 'moved or rearranged' touches 'intervention and counterfactual reasoning'.

'Concentrate on a task over a period of time without being distracted' is sustained attention, which no definition describes; Metacognitive & Supervisory covers 'plausibility auditing' and 'problem formulation', not concentration.
'Shift back and forth between two or more activities or sources of information' is attention switching, which no definition describes, including 'plausibility auditing' or 'problem formulation'.
'Keep your hand and arm steady while moving your arm or while holding your arm and hand in one position' is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Quickly move your hand ... to grasp, manipulate, or assemble objects' is plainly 'physical skill'.
'Precisely coordinated movements of the fingers ... to grasp, manipulate, or assemble very small objects' is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Quickly and repeatedly adjust the controls of a machine or a vehicle to exact positions' is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Coordinate two or more limbs' while sitting, standing, or lying down is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Choose quickly between two or more movements in response to two or more different signals', started 'with the hand, foot, or other body part', is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Time your movements ... in anticipation of changes in the speed and/or direction of a moving object' is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence', and the 'anticipation' also touches 'prediction'.
'Quickly respond (with the hand, finger, or foot) to a signal (sound, light, picture)' is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Make fast, simple, repeated movements of the fingers, hands, and wrists' is plainly 'physical skill'.
'Quickly move the arms and legs' is plainly 'physical skill'.
'Exert maximum muscle force to lift, push, pull, or carry objects' is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Use short bursts of muscle force to propel oneself ... or to throw an object' is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Exert muscle force repeatedly or continuously over time', meaning 'muscular endurance', is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Use your abdominal and lower back muscles to support part of the body' without fatiguing is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Exert yourself physically over long periods of time without getting winded' is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Bend, stretch, twist, or reach with your body, arms, and/or legs' is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Quickly and repeatedly bend, stretch, twist, or reach out with your body, arms, and/or legs' is a bodily capacity plainly covered by 'physical skill'.
'Coordinate the movement of your arms, legs, and torso together when the whole body is in motion' is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Keep or regain your body balance or stay upright when in an unstable position' is plainly 'physical skill and sensorimotor intelligence'.
'See details at close range' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'See details at a distance' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Match or detect differences between colors, including shades of color and brightness' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'See under low-light conditions' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'See objects or movement of objects to one's side when the eyes are looking ahead' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Judge which of several objects is closer or farther away from you, or ... the distance between you and an object' is plainly 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'See objects in the presence of a glare or bright lighting' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Detect or tell the differences between sounds that vary in pitch and loudness' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Focus on a single source of sound in the presence of other distracting sounds' is auditory perception plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.
'Tell the direction from which a sound originated' is a sensory capacity plainly covered by 'sensorimotor intelligence'.

'Identify ... the speech of another person' is 'classification' by 'pattern-matching' and perceiving speech is 'sensorimotor intelligence', but 'understand' the speech is not covered by either definition.
'Speak clearly' is a motor act covered by 'physical skill', but the communicative aim 'so others can understand you' is not covered by the definition.
